a clinical suspicion of a mAID is mandatory to perform genetic testing, and that genetic testing is essential to identify a specific mAID in adult patients with periodic febrile symptoms.

the most important clinical and genetic clues for the diagnosis of an mAID are: (i) the age at onset of symptoms; (ii) the presence of fever, skin rash, abdominal symptoms, joint involvement; (iii) the absence of infection or autoimmunity; and (iv) the family history of periodic fever.

, in the absence of any other cause of fever, a genetic analysis of the most frequent mAIDs should be performed in any adult patient with recurrent fever, regardless of the presence of any other clinical sign.

adult onset mAID patients should be screened for the most frequent genetic causes of periodic fevers and for the most common clinical presentations of the most frequent genetic forms of hereditary periodic fevers.

The main takeaway from our work is that
adult onset mAID patients should be screened for the most frequent mutations in the Mediterranean area, i.e., MEFV, TNFRSF1A, NLRP3 and MVK genes.
